C₆H₅COOH (benzoic acid). HCOOH is aliphatic; C₆H₅OH is phenol and C₆H₅CH₂OH benzyl alcohol.

In methanol CH₃OH the carbon has four single bonds, so it is sp³-hybridised.

Acid halides, anhydrides, esters and amides all give back the carboxylic acid on hydrolysis (reaction with water, often with acid or base).

shortQuestions: Pure (anhydrous) acetic acid freezes at 16.6 °C.
In cold weather it solidifies into colourless, ice-like crystals (glacies = ice), so it is called glacial acetic acid.
The –COOH group has a strongly polar O–H and a C=O that accepts hydrogen bonds, so two acid molecules join by two hydrogen bonds to form a cyclic dimer.

These strong double hydrogen bonds (which persist even in the vapour) need more energy to break than the single hydrogen bonds in alcohols, so carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols of similar molecular mass (acetic acid 118 °C, propan-1-ol 97 °C).
In the carboxylate ion RCOO⁻ the negative charge is shared equally between two oxygen atoms by resonance (two equivalent structures), which strongly stabilises it.
In the phenoxide ion the charge is delocalised onto ring carbons, which is less effective; in water (OH⁻) and alkoxide ions (RO⁻) there is no resonance (and alkyl groups even destabilise RO⁻).
So acid strength: RCOOH (pKa ≈ 4–5) > phenol (≈ 10) > water (15.7) > alcohols (≈ 16–18).
In ethanoic acid the methyl group releases electrons (+I effect), which intensifies the negative charge on the ethanoate ion and makes the O–H bond less polar.
Methanoic acid has only H on the carboxyl carbon, so its anion is more stable and it ionises more: pKa 3.75 (methanoic) vs 4.76 (ethanoic).
Chlorine is highly electronegative and withdraws electrons through the C–C bond (−I effect).
This disperses the negative charge of the chloroacetate ion (stabilising it) and makes the O–H bond more polar, so H⁺ is released more readily: pKa 2.86 compared with 4.76 for acetic acid.
A primary alcohol is first oxidised to an aldehyde, which is itself easily oxidised further to the carboxylic acid: RCH₂OH + [O] → RCHO + H₂O; RCHO + [O] → RCOOH.
Heating under reflux with excess strong oxidant (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄) keeps the aldehyde in the flask so that it is converted completely into the acid, e.g. CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOH.
In a carboxylic acid the lone pair on the –OH oxygen is delocalised into the C=O group by resonance (O=C–OH ↔ ⁻O–C=OH⁺), which reduces the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.

Also, basic nucleophiles simply remove the acidic proton to form the carboxylate ion, whose negative charge repels further nucleophilic attack. So acids are less reactive than aldehydes towards nucleophiles.
In an amide the lone pair on nitrogen is strongly delocalised into the carbonyl group (resonance O=C–NH₂ ↔ ⁻O–C=NH₂⁺), so the carbonyl carbon is only weakly electrophilic.
In addition, NH₂⁻ is a very strong base and therefore a very poor leaving group. Hence amides are the least reactive acid derivatives.
Fats and oils are esters of glycerol with long-chain fatty acids. Boiling them with NaOH (or KOH) hydrolyses them to glycerol and the sodium salts of the fatty acids — which are soaps.
So alkaline hydrolysis of esters is called saponification (Latin sapo = soap). It goes to completion because the carboxylate ion formed does not react back with the alcohol.

Chlorine is strongly electronegative, so it withdraws electrons and makes the carbonyl carbon highly electrophilic; its lone pairs donate very little back by resonance (poor overlap of Cl 3p with C 2p).
Cl⁻ is a very weak base and therefore an excellent leaving group. So acid halides react fastest: acid halides > anhydrides > esters > amides.
longQuestions: Carboxylic acids are weak acids: RCOOH + H₂O ⇌ RCOO⁻ + H₃O⁺ (Ka ≈ 10⁻⁵, e.g. acetic acid pKa 4.76). Their acidity comes from the polar O–H bond and especially from resonance stabilisation of the carboxylate ion, whose negative charge is spread equally over two oxygen atoms (both C–O bonds 127 pm).
They turn blue litmus red, react with metals (H₂), bases and even NaHCO₃ (liberating CO₂), so they are stronger than phenols and alcohols.

Electron-withdrawing substituents (–F, –Cl, –Br, –NO₂, –CN) increase acid strength by the −I effect, dispersing the negative charge: CH₃COOH (4.76) < ClCH₂COOH (2.86) < Cl₂CHCOOH (1.29) < Cl₃CCOOH (0.65); FCH₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > BrCH₂COOH > ICH₂COOH. The effect weakens with distance (2-chlorobutanoic > 3-chlorobutanoic > 4-chlorobutanoic).

Electron-donating (alkyl) groups decrease acid strength (+I effect): HCOOH (3.75) > CH₃COOH (4.76) > CH₃CH₂COOH (4.87). In benzoic acids, p-nitrobenzoic acid is stronger and p-methylbenzoic acid weaker than benzoic acid (4.2).
i. From a nitrile (acid hydrolysis): CH₃C≡N + 2H₂O —H⁺→ CH₃COOH + NH₄⁺.
ii. From a Grignard reagent and CO₂, then hydrolysis: CH₃MgBr + CO₂ → CH₃COOMgBr —H₃O⁺→ CH₃COOH + Mg(OH)Br.
iii. From an alcohol (oxidation): CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] —K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, reflux→ CH₃COOH + H₂O.
iv. From an aldehyde (oxidation): CH₃CHO + [O] —K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄→ CH₃COOH.
v. From an acid halide (hydrolysis): CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl.
i. Acetyl chloride: CH₃COOH + SOCl₂ → CH₃COCl + SO₂ + HCl (or 3CH₃COOH + PCl₃ → 3CH₃COCl + H₃PO₃).
ii. Acetic anhydride: heat acetic acid with P₂O₅: 2CH₃COOH → (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O; or CH₃COCl + CH₃COONa → (CH₃CO)₂O + NaCl.
iii. Acetamide: CH₃COOH + NH₃ → CH₃COONH₄, then heat: CH₃COONH₄ → CH₃CONH₂ + H₂O.
iv. Ethyl acetate: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ (conc. H₂SO₄) CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.
v. Ethyl alcohol: reduction with lithium aluminium hydride: CH₃COOH + 4[H] —LiAlH₄→ CH₃CH₂OH + H₂O.
i. Hydrolysis of acetyl chloride: CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl.
ii. Benzoyl chloride with methanol: C₆H₅COCl + CH₃OH → C₆H₅COOCH₃ (methyl benzoate) + HCl.
iii. Butan-1-ol with acetic anhydride: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH + (CH₃CO)₂O → CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ (butyl acetate) + CH₃COOH.
iv. Ammonolysis of butanoyl chloride: CH₃CH₂CH₂COCl + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂CH₂CONH₂ (butanamide) + NH₄Cl.
v. Fischer esterification of pentanoic acid with ethanol: CH₃(CH₂)₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ (conc. H₂SO₄) CH₃(CH₂)₃COOC₂H₅ (ethyl pentanoate) + H₂O.

(a) Preparation of carboxylic acids: (i) oxidation of primary alcohols or aldehydes with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄: RCH₂OH → RCOOH; (ii) hydrolysis of nitriles: RC≡N + 2H₂O + H⁺ → RCOOH + NH₄⁺; (iii) carbonation of Grignard reagents: RMgX + CO₂ → RCOOMgX → (H₃O⁺) RCOOH. (Also oxidation of alkylbenzenes: C₆H₅CH₃ + 3[O] —KMnO₄→ C₆H₅COOH + H₂O.)

(b, c) Structural formulas: i. 3-ethyl-4-methylpentanoic acid: HOOC–CH₂–CH(C₂H₅)–CH(CH₃)–CH₃. ii. Ethyl 3-methylbutanoate: (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–COO–C₂H₅. iii. 2-Chloropropanoyl bromide: CH₃–CHCl–COBr. iv. Ethanoic propanoic anhydride: CH₃CO–O–COCH₂CH₃. v. 3,3-Dimethylbutanenitrile: (CH₃)₃C–CH₂–C≡N. (Part (b) prints no structures to be named.)

(d) i. CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃CH₂CH₂COCl + POCl₃ + HCl. ii. CH₃CH₂COOH + SOCl₂ → CH₃CH₂COCl + SO₂ + HCl. iii. CH₃CH₂CONH₂ + 4[H] (LiAlH₄) → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ + H₂O. iv. CH₃COOCOCH₃ + NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + CH₃COOH (with excess NH₃ the acid becomes CH₃COONH₄).

v. CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ + NaOH → CH₃CH₂COONa + CH₃OH. vi. CH₃CH₂COONa + NaOH —CaO, heat→ CH₃CH₃ + Na₂CO₃ (decarboxylation). vii. CH₃CH₂COOC₂H₅ + 4[H] (LiAlH₄) → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + C₂H₅OH. viii. CH₃CH₂MgBr + CH₃CH₂C≡N → (CH₃CH₂)₂C=NMgBr, which on hydrolysis (H₃O⁺) gives CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ (pentan-3-one) + NH₃ + Mg(OH)Br.
activities: Observation: brisk effervescence (bubbles of gas) as soon as the acid is added to sodium hydrogencarbonate solution; the gas turns lime water milky, showing it is CO₂.
Equation: RCOOH + NaHCO₃ → RCOONa + H₂O + CO₂↑ (e.g. CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂).
Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than carbonic acid, so they liberate CO₂; phenols and alcohols are weaker and give no bubbles. This test distinguishes carboxylic acids from them.
